First (<reference osisRef="Amos.7.1-Amos.7.9">Am 7:1-9</reference>): Prophecies Illustrated by Three Symbols: (1) A vision of grasshoppers or young locusts, which devour the grass, but are removed at Amos' entreaty; (2) Fire drying up even the deep, and withering part of the land, but removed at Amos' entreaty; (3) A plumb-line to mark the buildings for destruction. They do not in the East mow their grass and make hay of it, but cut it off the ground as they require it.<div eID="gen23252" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23253" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the king's mowings--</hi>the first-fruits of the mown grass, tyrannically exacted by the king from the people. entries.content_plain: CHAPTER 7 Am. 7:1-9 . The seventh, eighth, and ninth chapters contain Visions, with Their Explanations. The seventh chapter consists of two parts. First ( Am 7:1-9 ): Prophecies Illustrated by Three Symbols: (1) A vision of grasshoppers or young locusts, which devour the grass, but are removed at Amos' entreaty; (2) Fire drying up even the deep, and withering part of the land, but removed at Amos' entreaty; (3) A plumb-line to mark the buildings for destruction. Secondly ( Am 7:10-17 ): Narrative of Amaziah's Interruption of Amos in Consequence of the Foregoing Prophecies, and Prediction of His Doom. 1. showed ... me; and, behold-- The same formula prefaces the three visions in this chapter, and the fourth in Am 8:1 . grasshoppers-- rather, "locusts" in the caterpillar state, from a Hebrew root, "to creep forth." In the autumn the eggs are deposited in the earth; in the spring the young come forth [Maurer]. the latter growth-- namely, of grass, which comes up after the mowing. They do not in the East mow their grass and make hay of it, but cut it off the ground as they require it. the king's mowings-- the first-fruits of the mown grass, tyrannically exacted by the king from the people. The literal locusts, as in Joel, are probably symbols of human foes: thus the "growth" of grass "after the king's mowings" will mean the political revival of Israel under Jeroboam II ( 2Ki 14:25 ), after it had been mown down, as it were, by Hazael and Ben-hadad of Syria ( 2Ki 13:3 ), [Grotius].

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12606"/><div sID="gen23256" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12606"/><hi type="bold">3. repented for this--</hi>that is, of this. The change was not in the mind of God (<reference osisRef="Num.2.19">Nu 2:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jas.1.17">Jas 1:17</reference>), but in the effect outwardly. God unchangeably does what is just; it is just that He should hear intercessory prayer (<reference osisRef="Jas.5.16-Jas.5.18">Jas 5:16-18</reference>), as it would have been just for Him to have let judgment take its course at once on the guilty nation, but for the prayer of one or two righteous men in it (compare <reference osisRef="Gen.18.23-Gen.18.33">Ge 18:23-33</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.11">1Sa 15:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.42.10">Jr 42:10</reference>). The repentance of the sinner, and God's regard to His own attributes of mercy and covenanted love, also cause God outwardly to deal with him as if he repented (<reference osisRef="Jonah.3.10">Jon 3:10</reference>), whereas the change in outward dealing is in strictest harmony with God's own unchangeableness.<div eID="gen23256" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23257" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">It shall not be--</hi>Israel's utter overthrow now. Pul was influenced by God to accept money and withdraw from Israel. <div eID="gen23257" type="x-p"/>

The repentance of the sinner, and God's regard to His own attributes of mercy and covenanted love, also cause God outwardly to deal with him as if he repented ( Jon 3:10 ), whereas the change in outward dealing is in strictest harmony with God's own unchangeableness. It shall not be-- Israel's utter overthrow now. Pul was influenced by God to accept money and withdraw from Israel.

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12609"/><div sID="gen23262" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12609"/><hi type="bold">8. plumb-line in ... midst of ... Israel--</hi>No longer are the symbols, as in the former two, stated generally; this one is expressly applied to Israel. God's long-suffering is worn out by Israel's perversity: so Amos ceases to intercede (compare <reference osisRef="Gen.18.33">Ge 18:33</reference>). The plummet line was used not only in building, but in destroying houses (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.21.13">2Ki 21:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.28.17">Is 28:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.34.11">34:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lam.2.8">La 2:8</reference>). It denotes that God's judgments are measured out by the most exact rules of justice. Here it is placed "in the midst" of Israel, that is, the judgment is not to be confined to an outer part of Israel, as by Tiglath-pileser; it is to reach the very center. This was fulfilled when Shalmaneser, after a three years' siege of Samaria, took it and carried away Israel captive finally to Assyria (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.17.3">2Ki 17:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.5.6">5, 6</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.5.23">23</reference>).<div eID="gen23262" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23263" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not ... pass by ... any more--</hi>not forgive them any more (<reference osisRef="Amos.8.2">Am 8:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.19.11">Pr 19:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.7.18">Mi 7:18</reference>). <div eID="gen23263" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12610"/><div sID="gen23264" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12610"/><hi type="bold">9. high places--</hi>dedicated to idols.<div eID="gen23264" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23265" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of Isaac--</hi>They boasted of their following the example of their forefather Isaac, in erecting high places at Beer-sheba (<reference osisRef="Amos.5.5">Am 5:5</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Gen.26.23">Ge 26:23</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.26.24">24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.46.1">46:1</reference>); but he and Abraham erected them before the temple was appointed at Jerusalem--and to God; whereas they did so, after the temple had been fixed as the only place for sacrifices--and to idols. In the Hebrew here "Isaac" is written with s, instead of the usual ts; both forms mean "laughter"; the change of spelling perhaps expresses that their "high places of Isaac" may be well so called, but not as they meant by the name; for they are only fit to be laughed at in scorn. Probably, however, the mention of "Isaac" and "Israel" simply expresses that these names, which their degenerate posterity boasted in as if ensuring their safety, will not save them and their idolatrous "sanctuaries" on which they depended from ruin (compare <reference osisRef="Amos.8.14">Am 8:14</reference>).<div eID="gen23265" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23266" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">house of Jeroboam with ... sword--</hi>fulfilled in the extinction of Zachariah, son of Jeroboam II, the last of the descendants of Jeroboam I, who had originated the idolatry of the calves (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.15.8-2Kgs.15.10">2Ki 15:8-10</reference>).<div eID="gen23266" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23267" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Amos.7.10-Amos.7.17">Am. 7:10-17</reference>. Amaziah's Charge against Amos: His Doom Foretold. <div eID="gen23267" type="x-p"/>

These being a device of state policy to keep Israel separate from Judah. Amaziah construes Amos words against them as treason. So in the case of Elijah and Jeremiah (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.17">1Ki 18:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.37.13">Jr 37:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.37.14">14</reference>). So the antitype Jesus was charged (<reference osisRef="John.19.12">Joh 19:12</reference>); political expediency being made in all ages the pretext for dishonoring God and persecuting His servants (<reference osisRef="John.11.48-John.11.50">Joh 11:48-50</reference>). So in the case of Paul (<reference osisRef="Acts.17.6">Ac 17:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.17.7">7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.24.5">24:5</reference>).<div eID="gen23268" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23269" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the midst of ... Israel--</hi>probably alluding to Amos' own words, "in the midst of ... Israel" (<reference osisRef="Amos.7.8">Am 7:8</reference>), foretelling the state's overthrow to the very center. Not secretly, or in a corner, but openly, in the very center of the state, so as to upset the whole utterly.<div eID="gen23269" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23270" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">land is not able to bear all his words--</hi>They are so many and so intolerable. I was no prophet--</hi>in answer to Amaziah's insinuation (<reference osisRef="Amos.7.12">Am 7:12</reference>), that he discharged the prophetical office to earn his "bread" (like Israel's mercenary prophets). So far from being rewarded, Jehovah's prophets had to expect imprisonment and even death as the result of their prophesying in Samaria or Israel: whereas the prophets of Baal were maintained at the king's expense (compare <reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.19">1Ki 18:19</reference>). I was not, says Amos, of the order of prophets, or educated in their schools, and deriving a livelihood from exercising the public functions of a prophet. I am a shepherd (compare <reference osisRef="Amos.7.15">Am 7:15</reference>, "flock"; the Hebrew for "herdsman" includes the meaning, shepherd, compare <reference osisRef="Amos.1.1">Am 1:1</reference>) in humble position, who did not even think of prophesying among you, until a divine call impelled me to it.<div eID="gen23279" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23280" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">prophet's son--</hi>that is, disciple. Schools of prophets are mentioned first in First Samuel; in these youths were educated to serve the theocracy as public instructors. Only in the kingdom of the ten tribes is the continuance of the schools of the prophets mentioned. They were missionary stations near the chief seats of superstition in Israel, and associations endowed with the Spirit of God; none were admitted but those to whom the Spirit had been previously imparted. Their spiritual fathers travelled about to visit the training schools, and cared for the members and even their widows (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.4.1">2Ki 4:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.2">2</reference>). The pupils had their common board in them, and after leaving them still continued members. The offerings which in Judah were given by the pious to the Levites, in Israel went to the schools of the prophets (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.4.42">2Ki 4:42</reference>). Prophecy (for example, Elijah and Elisha) in Israel was more connected with extraordinary events than in Judah, inasmuch as, in the absence of the legal hierarchy of the latter, it needed to have more palpable divine sanction.<div eID="gen23280" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23281" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sycamore--</hi>abounding in Palestine. The fruit was like the fig, but inferior; according to Pliny, a sort of compound, as the name expresses, of the fig and the mulberry. It was only eaten by the poorest (compare <reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.27">1Ki 10:27</reference>).<div eID="gen23281" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23282" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">gatherer--</hi>one occupied with their cultivation [Maurer]. To cultivate it, an incision was made in the fruit when of a certain size, and on the fourth day afterwards it ripened [Pliny, Natural History, 13.7,14]. Grotius from Jerome says, if it be not plucked off and "gathered" (which favors English Version), it is spoiled by gnats. <div eID="gen23282" type="x-p"/>
